title: CDC Vaccine Schedule Overhaul Leaves Parents Navigating a New Normal
excerpt: Seven months after the CDC cut recommended childhood vaccines from 17 to 11, pediatricians say families must be more proactive than ever about immunization decisions.
body:
• The CDC reduced recommended childhood vaccines from 17 to 11 in January 2026, moving six vaccines to "shared clinical decision-making" status
  • The AAP continues to recommend all 18 original vaccines and has issued its own 2026 schedule endorsed by 12 medical organizations
  • Pediatricians warn that declining vaccination rates have already triggered measles outbreaks across the U.S., with over 1,000 cases reported in 2025
  • Indian American families who travel to India face added complexity, as India's immunization schedule differs significantly from both the old and new U.S. guidelines

As the back-to-school season begins, American parents face a question that would have been unthinkable a year ago: which childhood vaccines should their children actually get?

On January 5, 2026, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention cut the number of universally recommended childhood vaccines from 17 to 11, acting on a presidential directive to align the U.S. schedule with those of other high-income nations. Vaccines for hepatitis A, hepatitis B, influenza, meningococcal disease, respiratory syncytial virus, and rotavirus were moved to a new category requiring "shared clinical decision-making" — conversations between parents and clinicians about individual risk.

Seven months later, pediatricians across the country say the policy shift has created confusion, longer clinic visits, and a widening gap between medical recommendations and federal guidance.

The Science Hasn't Changed

"The underlying science hasn't changed," said Dr. Charles Whittaker, assistant professor of infectious diseases and vaccinology at UC Berkeley School of Public Health. "The vaccines have been rigorously tested. Their safety and effectiveness have been affirmed through decades of real-world use and ongoing monitoring."

Whittaker was critical of the process behind the changes. "Major changes to a national immunization schedule do happen. But the changes are usually debated in public with input from pediatricians, immunologists, epidemiologists," he told Medical Xpress. "We just didn't see that kind of open process here."

The American Academy of Pediatrics responded by issuing its own 2026 immunization schedule on January 26, continuing to recommend routine immunization against all 18 diseases. The AAP schedule was endorsed by 12 medical organizations, including the American Medical Association, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and the Infectious Diseases Society of America.

"The AAP will continue to provide recommendations for immunizations that are rooted in science and are in the best interest of the health of infants, children and adolescents of this country."

— Dr. Andrew Racine, AAP President

What 'Shared Decision-Making' Means in Practice

The CDC's new framework groups vaccines into three categories: universally recommended, recommended for high-risk groups, and recommended through shared clinical decision-making. The third category requires parents to initiate conversations with clinicians — a shift that concerns pediatricians.

"When something moves out of the 'routine' bucket, it can get less airtime in a busy clinic," Whittaker warned. He advised parents to ask directly: "Are we following the AAP schedule, and are there vaccines we should still do even if they're not universal on the CDC list?"

Dr. Jennifer Dwyer, chief of primary care at Akron Children's, echoed the concern. "More time will be spent during the primary care visit explaining the importance of the vaccines than was required previously," she said. "This could take time away from other important health maintenance topics such as nutrition, behavior, safety, sleep, development."

HHS has instructed insurers to continue reimbursing all previously recommended vaccinations through 2026, meaning families should not face out-of-pocket costs for any of the reclassified vaccines.

Outbreaks Underscore the Stakes

The timing is fraught. The U.S. recorded over 1,000 measles cases by May 2025, and outbreaks have continued into 2026. Michigan alone has reported two measles outbreaks this year, accounting for 78% of the state's cases. The state's school vaccine waiver rate hit 6.2% in 2024 — the highest since 2013.

Dr. Mundeep Kaur Kainth, a pediatric infectious disease specialist at Northwell Health, noted that vaccines are "victims of their own success." An entire generation of parents has never seen polio or measles firsthand. "They don't feel the same urgency to vaccinate," she said.

Data from the AAP shows that between 1994 and 2023, vaccines prevented an estimated 1.13 million deaths, 508 million illnesses, and 32 million hospitalizations among U.S. children.

For Indian American Families, Added Layers of Complexity

Indian American parents navigating the new landscape face particular challenges. India's Universal Immunisation Programme follows a different schedule — the first measles-rubella dose is given at 9 months rather than 12, and the hepatitis B birth dose remains standard. Families who travel between the U.S. and India need to reconcile two diverging systems, especially now that the CDC has moved hepatitis A and B vaccines out of the universal category.

Hepatitis B is endemic in parts of South Asia, making the birth dose especially important for families with ties to the region. Dr. Seth Hoffman, an infectious disease specialist at Stanford Medicine, emphasized the stakes: "The birth dose of hepatitis B can prevent the development of a chronic infection that we cannot cure." He added that weakening the universal recommendation "means we're making a decision that we're OK with kids slipping through the cracks."

"Comparing the U.S. childhood immunization schedule to that of Denmark or other countries ignores fundamental differences in population size, diversity, healthcare access, and infectious disease risk."

— Dr. Phyllis Hopkins, via AJMC

What Parents Should Do Now

Pediatricians offer consistent advice: follow the AAP's 2026 schedule, not just the CDC's reduced recommendations. Parents should proactively ask their pediatrician about vaccines that have been reclassified rather than assuming they are no longer needed.

For families planning international travel — particularly to South Asia — clinicians recommend discussing hepatitis A and B vaccination before departure. Adolescents heading to college dormitories or communal living should discuss meningococcal vaccination timing. Pregnant women should consult their obstetrician about RSV maternal immunization.

Dr. Whittaker put it simply: "If your family has been vaccinating on schedule, there's no scientific reason to stop doing that now."
